independent_deductions: For f(x)=ln(x)/x on x>0, fprime=(1-ln(x))/x² gives the unique global maximum value 1/e at x=e. Distinguish the maximizing input, maximum output and point (e,1/e). Figure 1 dashed guides show those distinct coordinates; the curve has no value at x=0 and approaches zero from above as x tends to infinity.

Figure 2 shows five interior stationary points: three peaks and two valleys; its highest peak is the global maximum and its included right endpoint is the global minimum. With no coordinate axes or numeric labels, do not invent their values. Comparing a complete candidate set establishes extrema only when attainment is established: continuity on a closed bounded interval is one sufficient setting, and nondifferentiable interior candidates must not be omitted in a general method.

Figure 3 is an open-topped cylinder with radius r and height h: volume V=πr²h and surface area S=πr²+2πrh (one disk and a rectangular side). Fix V>0 and r>0, then h=V/(πr²), S(r)=πr²+2V/r. The source first writes h=V/(2πr), an error contradicted by its adjacent correct substitution. r=0 is inadmissible; infinity is not an endpoint in the domain.

Sprime=2πr-2V/r²=2(πr³-V)/r², hence the only critical radius rstar=(V/π)^(1/3). The derivative is negative below rstar and positive above it, proving a global minimum. Alternatively Sdoubleprime=2π+4V/r³>0 and the two boundary limits tend to positive infinity. hstar=rstar, and Smin=3π^(1/3)V^(2/3). Taking V=π gives r=h=1 and S=3π directly. The source surface-area substitution wrongly uses the positive instead of negative one-third power in its second term and then wrongly gives π^(-1/3) in the final answer. Source prose also drops V from 2V/r. Its assertion that S achieves both a maximum and a minimum is false: no maximum exists.

Figure 4 encodes decreasing then increasing area with both tails unbounded and a finite minimum, not included infinite endpoints. The minimum location is a feasible radius, with height and area obtained from the original physical quantities. Dimensional homogeneity alone does not catch the incorrect dimensionless power of π; independent substitution does.

For unit wire split into lengths x and 1-x, the square sides are x/4 and (1-x)/4, so A(x)=[x²+(1-x)²]/16=(x-1/2)²/8+1/32. Aprime=x/8-(1-x)/8=x/4-1/8=(2x-1)/8 and Adoubleprime=1/4. The source derivative line visibly contains the false middle simplification x/8-x/8+1/8 even though its eventual stationary equation 2x-1=0 and result x=1/2 are correct. The author must calculate rather than copy this line.

The minimum 1/32 is attained at x=1/2 for both domains (0,1) and [0,1]. On [0,1], the maximum 1/16 is attained at x=0 and x=1, representing one square and a zero-length second piece. If two positive pieces are mandatory, the domain is (0,1); A(x)<1/16 and values approach 1/16 but no maximum is attained. The final source prose explicitly makes this qualification. Figure 5 is miscaptioned Example 5 although it illustrates Example 4. Figure 6 uses hollow markers also at the attained minimum, so these markers cannot silently be read as deleting the polynomial point; endpoint inclusion must be stated through the model.
